nodes.label: Electrostatics and Capacitance
nodes.note: Electrostatics builds from one force law into field, potential, dipole, Gauss, and finally capacitors. The spine of the chapter is $$\vec{F} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}\hat{r}$$.

nodes.label: Charge and Coulomb's Law
nodes.note: Charge comes in integer units of $$e$$ and obeys an inverse-square force between resting point charges. Everything downstream starts here.

nodes.label: Quantization and Conservation of Charge
nodes.note: Any isolated charge is an integer multiple of the elementary charge: $$q = \pm ne$$ for $$n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$$. Charge can only move between bodies, so the total of an isolated system stays fixed.

nodes.label: Coulomb's Law
nodes.note: Two point charges pull or push along the line joining them with magnitude $$F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$$. The constant evaluates to $$k = 9 \times 10^9\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$$.

nodes.label: Force in a Dielectric Medium
nodes.note: A medium of dielectric constant $$K$$ weakens the force between fixed charges because bound charge screens them. The reduction is $$F_{med} = \frac{F_{vac}}{K}$$.

nodes.label: Superposition of Electrostatic Forces
nodes.note: Each pair contributes independently, so net force is the vector sum over all partners: $$\vec{F}_{net} = \sum_{i} \vec{F}_i$$. Resolve into components before adding; the forces are never collinear in JEE setups.

nodes.label: Permittivity of Free Space
nodes.note: Permittivity fixes the strength of electric interactions in vacuum: $$\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{F/m}$$. It is bundled into $$k = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$$ to shorten algebra.

nodes.label: Electric Field and Field Lines
nodes.note: The field is force per unit test charge, so it exists even with no charge present. Standard geometries give closed-form results such as $$E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$$.

nodes.label: Definition of Electric Field
nodes.note: The field is defined by a vanishing test charge so the source is undisturbed: $$\vec{E} = \lim_{q_0 \to 0}\frac{\vec{F}}{q_0}$$. Field vectors from several sources add like any vectors.

nodes.label: Field of an Infinite Line Charge
nodes.note: Cylindrical symmetry makes Gauss's law trivial for linear density $$\lambda$$, giving a field that falls as $$1/r$$. The result is $$E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$$, or $$E = \frac{2k\lambda}{r}$$.

nodes.label: Field on the Axis of a Charged Ring
nodes.note: Off-axis components cancel and the axial field peaks at a finite distance. It reads $$E(x) = \frac{kQx}{(x^2 + R^2)^{3/2}}$$, with maximum at $$x = \frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$$.

nodes.label: Field of a Uniformly Charged Disc
nodes.note: A disc is a stack of rings, and its field rises from zero at the centre to the sheet value far away. The closed form is $$E(x) = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(1 - \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + R^2}}\right)$$.

nodes.label: Field of Charged Spheres
nodes.note: A shell shields its interior, while a solid sphere's enclosed charge grows with $$r$$. Outside both, $$E = \frac{kQ}{r^2}$$, inside a solid sphere $$E = \frac{kQr}{R^3}$$, and inside a shell $$E = 0$$.

nodes.label: Field of Infinite Charged Sheets
nodes.note: A non-conducting sheet sends the same field to both sides, independent of distance: $$E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$$. Just outside a charged conductor the field doubles to $$E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$$.

nodes.label: Potential and Potential Energy
nodes.note: Potential trades vectors for scalars, since it stores the work done against the field. The link to field is $$\Delta V = -\int \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r}$$.

nodes.label: Potential Difference
nodes.note: Potential difference is work per unit charge moved by an external agent against the field: $$\Delta V = V_B - V_A = \frac{W_{ext}}{q}$$. The minus sign in $$\vec{E} = -\nabla V$$ says field points down the potential slope.

nodes.label: Potential of Standard Geometries
nodes.note: Scalars superpose directly, so a shell gives $$V = \frac{kQ}{r}$$ outside and $$V = \frac{kQ}{R}$$ throughout. Inside a solid sphere $$V(r) = \frac{kQ}{2R^3}(3R^2 - r^2)$$, maximum at the centre.

nodes.label: Equipotential Surfaces
nodes.note: Moving a charge on an equipotential costs nothing, so field lines meet these surfaces at right angles. Numerically $$W = q\Delta V = 0$$, and the field strength along the normal is $$E = -\frac{dV}{dr}$$.

nodes.label: Electrostatic Potential Energy of a System
nodes.note: Assembling a charge distribution costs energy pair by pair: $$U = \sum_{i < j}\frac{kq_i q_j}{r_{ij}} = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i q_i V_i$$. The factor of half avoids double counting each pair.

nodes.label: Work Done by an External Agent
nodes.note: The electrostatic force is conservative, so work depends only on endpoints: $$W_{ext} = \Delta U = q(V_f - V_i)$$. Kinetic energy then comes from $$\Delta K = -\Delta U$$ when released.

nodes.label: Electric Dipole
nodes.note: Two equal opposite charges separated by a small distance form the standard non-uniform field source. Its strength is $$\vec{p} = q(2\vec{a})$$.

nodes.label: Dipole Moment
nodes.note: Dipole moment points from the negative to the positive charge with magnitude charge times separation: $$\vec{p} = q(2\vec{a})$$. Far-field formulas assume $$r \gg a$$ throughout.

nodes.label: Axial and Equatorial Fields
nodes.note: On the axis the dipole field runs along $$\vec{p}$$ while on the equatorial plane it runs opposite: $$E_{axial} = \frac{2kp}{r^3}$$ and $$E_{eq} = -\frac{kp}{r^3}$$. The axial value is exactly twice the equatorial one at equal distance.

nodes.label: Field and Potential at a General Point
nodes.note: At angle $$\theta$$ from the axis the components combine as $$E = \frac{kp}{r^3}\sqrt{1 + 3\cos^2\theta}$$, while potential is $$V = \frac{kp\cos\theta}{r^2}$$. The equatorial plane stays at $$V = 0$$ everywhere.

nodes.label: Torque and Energy in an External Field
nodes.note: A uniform field exerts no net force but does torque the dipole toward alignment: $$\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}$$ with $$\tau = pE\sin\theta$$. Its potential energy is $$U = -\vec{p}\cdot\vec{E} = -pE\cos\theta$$.

nodes.label: Angular Oscillation of a Dipole
nodes.note: Released near alignment the restoring torque makes simple harmonic motion for small angles. The period is $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{pE}}$$ with $$I$$ the moment of inertia.

nodes.label: Gauss's Law and Conductors
nodes.note: Gauss's law converts hard integrals into bookkeeping of enclosed charge: $$\Phi_E = \frac{q_{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}$$. It also fixes how charge sits on a conductor at rest.

nodes.label: Gauss's Theorem
nodes.note: Total flux through any closed surface depends only on the charge inside it, never on the surface shape: $$\Phi_E = \oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{q_{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}$$. Choose a surface matching the symmetry of the source.

nodes.label: Flux Through Symmetric Portions
nodes.note: When a charge sits at a symmetric point, flux splits evenly among the pieces seen from it. A charge at a cube corner leaks $$\Phi = \frac{q}{8\varepsilon_0}$$ through that cube, and one at the centre gives $$\frac{q}{6\varepsilon_0}$$ per face.

nodes.label: Electrostatic Equilibrium of Conductors
nodes.note: Free charges rearrange until the bulk field vanishes and all excess charge lives on the surface. Just outside the surface $$E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$$, and the whole conductor sits at one potential.

nodes.label: Electrostatic Shielding
nodes.note: A Gaussian surface inside conductor material carries no flux, so a cavity with no charge is field-free: $$E_{cavity} = 0$$. This is why instruments are housed in metal enclosures.

nodes.label: Electrostatic Pressure on a Surface
nodes.note: Each surface element is pulled outward by the field of the rest of the charge, which is half the total field. The resulting pressure is $$P = \frac{\sigma^2}{2\varepsilon_0} = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$$.

nodes.label: Capacitors
nodes.note: A capacitor stores separated charge at a fixed ratio set by geometry, not by charge: $$C = \frac{Q}{V}$$. Networks then combine exactly like resistors, but inverted.

nodes.label: Capacitance Definition
nodes.note: Capacitance measures charge stored per volt and depends only on shape, size, and medium: $$C = \frac{Q}{V}$$. An isolated sphere of radius $$R$$ is a capacitor with $$C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 R$$.

nodes.label: Standard Capacitances
nodes.note: Parallel plates give $$C_0 = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$$, while concentric shells of radii $$a < b$$ give $$C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0\frac{ab}{b - a}$$. Coaxial cylinders of length $$L$$ give $$C = \frac{2\pi\varepsilon_0 L}{\ln(b/a)}$$.

nodes.label: Energy Stored in a Capacitor
nodes.note: Building up the charge costs work that ends up in the field: $$U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 = \frac{Q^2}{2C}$$. That energy lives in space as density $$u = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$$.

nodes.label: Force Between the Plates
nodes.note: Each plate feels only the field of the other, which is half the total field, so a factor of half appears. The attraction is $$F = \frac{Q^2}{2\varepsilon_0 A} = \frac{1}{2}QE$$.

nodes.label: Capacitor Networks
nodes.note: Series capacitors share charge while parallel capacitors share voltage, inverting the resistor rules. Balanced ladders and infinite grids reduce to these two cases.

nodes.label: Series Combination
nodes.note: In series every capacitor carries the same charge $$Q$$ while voltages split: $$\frac{1}{C_{eq}} = \sum_i \frac{1}{C_i}$$. The equivalent capacitance is always smaller than the smallest member.

nodes.label: Parallel Combination
nodes.note: In parallel every capacitor sees the same voltage and charges simply add: $$C_{eq} = \sum_i C_i$$. Charge divides in proportion to capacitance, $$Q_i = C_i V$$.

nodes.label: Dielectrics and Charge Sharing
nodes.note: Inserting an insulator raises capacitance and lowers the internal field, and the boundary conditions decide whether charge or voltage is fixed. The rule of thumb is $$C \to KC_0$$.

nodes.label: Partially Filled Dielectric Slab
nodes.note: A slab of thickness $$t$$ and constant $$K$$ shortens the effective gap of the capacitor. The capacitance becomes $$C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d - t\left(1 - \frac{1}{K}\right)}$$, and a conductor slab is the limit $$K \to \infty$$.

nodes.label: Field Inside a Dielectric
nodes.note: Polarization produces an opposing field that reduces the applied one: $$E_{in} = \frac{E_0}{K}$$. The material response is $$K = 1 + \chi_e$$ with susceptibility $$\chi_e$$.

nodes.label: Battery Disconnected or Connected
nodes.note: With the battery removed charge is trapped, so inserting the slab drops energy: $$U_{disc} = \frac{U_0}{K}$$. With the battery kept the voltage is pinned and energy rises: $$U_{conn} = K U_0$$, the surplus supplied by the battery.

nodes.label: Charge Sharing and Energy Loss
nodes.note: Connecting charged capacitors equalizes voltage at $$V_{common} = \frac{C_1V_1 + C_2V_2}{C_1 + C_2}$$ while total charge is conserved. The missing energy leaves as heat: $$\Delta H = \frac{C_1 C_2 (V_1 - V_2)^2}{2(C_1 + C_2)}$$.

nodes.label: Energy Density with a Dielectric
nodes.note: Inside the filled region the field is weaker but permittivity is higher, and the product sets the stored density. It reads $$u = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 K E_{in}^2 = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E_0 E_{in}$$.
